```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 110)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))

rd <- function(f) if (file.exists(f)) read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                                              check.names = FALSE) else NULL
bench   <- rd("scores/benchmark_summary.csv")
abl     <- rd("scores/ablation_summary.csv")
recall  <- rd("scores/pathway_recall.csv")
gt      <- read.csv("ground_truth.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)

MODELS <- c("deepseek-flash", "deepseek-v4-pro")
N_CELLS <- nrow(gt) * length(MODELS)
N_DONE  <- if (is.null(bench)) 0 else nrow(bench)

ora <- if (!is.null(recall)) recall[recall$arm == "ORA_only", ] else NULL
llm <- if (!is.null(recall)) recall[recall$arm == "LLM", ] else NULL
```

# 0. Run status

This report renders itself from whatever is on disk, so it is always honest
about coverage: every table states how many of the planned
`r nrow(gt)` × `r length(MODELS)` = `r N_CELLS` dataset-model cells are
actually filled. Nothing is imputed.

```{r}
grid <- expand.grid(dataset = gt$dataset_id, model = MODELS,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grid$status <- ifelse(
  paste(grid$dataset, grid$model) %in%
    paste(bench$dataset, bench$model), "complete", "pending")
grid$status <- factor(grid$status, levels = c("complete", "pending"))
knitr::kable(
  xtabs(~ dataset + model, grid) ,
  caption = "Planned benchmark grid (count of datasets per cell).")
tab <- reshape(grid, idvar = "dataset", timevar = "model", direction = "wide")
names(tab) <- sub("status\\.", "", names(tab))
knitr::kable(tab, caption = sprintf(
  "Cell-level status: %d of %d runs complete.", N_DONE, N_CELLS))
```

```{r}
if (N_DONE < N_CELLS) {
  cat(sprintf("\n> **Partial grid.** %d of %d runs have been executed. All\n",
              N_DONE, N_CELLS),
      "> quantitative claims below are computed only over completed runs;\n",
      "> the remaining cells are produced by `benchmark/02_run_benchmark.R`\n",
      "> once API credit is available. Sections that do not depend on the LLM\n",
      "> (data preparation, ORA baseline) are complete for all datasets.\n")
}
```

# 1. What is being measured

The usual way to evaluate an LLM in bioinformatics is to ask whether the
output "looks right". That is not falsifiable. This benchmark instead uses
perturbation experiments whose mechanism is known *independently of the
transcriptome*: the drug's target, the receptor it engages, or the gene that
was knocked out. For each dataset the mechanism is written down as three
components **before** any model is run, and every interpretation is scored
against that fixed text.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(dataset = gt$dataset_id, GEO = gt$gse,
             perturbation = gt$perturbagen, system = gt$cell_type,
             `pre-registered mechanism` = gsub("\\|", "; ", gt$gt_components),
             check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Benchmark datasets. `gt_components` is fixed in ground_truth.csv and is never edited after seeing model output.")
```

Three quantities are reported for every run:

| quantity | definition | cost |
|---|---|---|
| **mechanism recovery** | fraction of the pre-registered components recovered, by a synonym-aware matcher over the full interpretation text | free |
| **hallucination rate** | fraction of cited pathways that appear in *neither* the input ORA table *nor* the controlled pathway vocabulary | free |
| **cost** | billed tokens × the provider's published per-token price (prompt and completion priced separately) | — |

A second, stricter recovery score is produced by an LLM judge that is always a
*different* model from the one being scored (cross-judging), which removes
self-preference bias without needing a third vendor.

## 1.1 The six perturbation datasets

```{r}
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(gt)), function(i) {
  f <- file.path("deg_tables", paste0(gt$dataset_id[i], ".rds"))
  if (!file.exists(f)) return(NULL)
  d <- readRDS(f)$deg
  sig <- !is.na(d$padj) & !is.na(d$log2FoldChange) &
    d$padj < 0.05 & abs(d$log2FoldChange) > 1
  data.frame(dataset = gt$dataset_id[i],
             genes_tested = nrow(d),
             strict_DEG = sum(sig, na.rm = TRUE),
             up = sum(sig & d$log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             down = sum(sig & d$log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             design = paste0(length(unique(readRDS(f)$treat_samples)), " vs ",
                             length(unique(readRDS(f)$ctrl_samples))))
})
deg_tab <- do.call(rbind, rows)
deg_tab$deg_mode <- ifelse(deg_tab$strict_DEG >= 20, "strict", "top-150 fallback")
knitr::kable(deg_tab, caption = "Differential-expression yield per dataset (padj < 0.05, |log2FC| > 1).")
```

Two design problems show up immediately and are handled explicitly rather
than hidden:

- **Underpowered contrasts.** Rapamycin in primary NK cells yields **zero**
  genes at the strict threshold. The pipeline therefore has an adaptive rule:
  if fewer than 20 genes pass, it falls back to the 150 smallest-p-value genes
  balanced by direction, and the fallback is recorded per run
  (`deg_mode` in `results/*.rds`). Two of the six datasets use it.
- **Panel-limited platforms.** The vorinostat table covers ~8,000 genes rather
  than the whole transcriptome, so its DEG count is not comparable in absolute
  terms. It is still usable because all metrics are ratios.

# 2. Does the LLM add anything over the enrichment table it was handed?

This is the first question a reviewer asks, and it can be answered **without
any API spend**, because the ORA table is exactly what the model sees as
input. Treat the top-*k* ORA terms as if they were the answer, score them
against the same ground truth, and you have the no-LLM control.

Both arms are scored through one projection: the pre-registered mechanism is
mapped, a priori, onto the 49 MSigDB-Hallmark-like terms shipped with the
package (`expected_gmt` in `ground_truth.csv`). Because the *same* projection
is used for the ORA arm and the LLM arm, any bias in the mapping cancels out
of the comparison.

```{r}
if (!is.null(ora)) {
  o <- ora[order(ora$dataset), ]
  o$recovered <- sprintf("%d/%d", o$n_expected_hit, o$n_expected)
  knitr::kable(
    o[, c("dataset", "deg_mode", "n_degs", "n_ora", "hit_at_5", "hit_at_10",
          "recovered", "rank_first_hit")],
    caption = "No-LLM control: how well does the ORA table alone recover the canonical pathways?")
  cat(sprintf(
    "\nAcross all %d datasets: **mean hit@5 = %.2f, mean hit@10 = %.2f**.\n",
    nrow(o), mean(o$hit_at_5), mean(o$hit_at_10)))
}
```

```{r fig.height=3.2}
if (!is.null(recall)) {
  pal <- c(ORA_only = "grey45", LLM = "#2c7fb8")
  ggplot(recall, aes(dataset, hit_at_5, fill = arm)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.72) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = pal, labels = c(ORA_only = "ORA table only",
                                               LLM = "LLM interpretation")) +
    coord_flip() + ylim(0, 1) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "canonical pathway recovered (top-5)", fill = NULL,
         title = "The enrichment table is already a strong baseline",
         subtitle = "ORA bars are complete for all 6 datasets; LLM bars only for completed runs")
}
```

The baseline is not a straw man: plain ORA recovers at least one canonical
pathway in the top five for two thirds of the datasets, and in the top ten for
five of six. **A credible claim for an LLM layer therefore cannot be "it finds
the pathway" — the pathway was already there.** What the model can add is the
part ORA cannot express: which pathway is causal, which is a passenger, how
the modules relate, what the direction means, and which follow-up experiment
would discriminate between the remaining hypotheses.

```{r}
if (!is.null(llm)) {
  m <- merge(
    aggregate(cbind(hit_at_5, n_expected_hit) ~ dataset, llm, mean),
    ora[, c("dataset", "hit_at_5", "n_expected_hit")],
    by = "dataset", suffixes = c("_llm", "_ora"))
  m$delta <- m$hit_at_5_llm - m$hit_at_5_ora
  knitr::kable(m, digits = 3,
    caption = "Pathway-level recall, LLM vs ORA-only, on the datasets where both exist.")
  cat(sprintf("\nMean change in pathway recall: **%+.2f** (n = %d datasets).\n",
              mean(m$delta), nrow(m)))
}
```

Reading the delta correctly matters. A near-zero or negative delta is a
*publishable* result, not a failed experiment: it says the LLM should be
scored on mechanism synthesis and auditability, and that benchmarking it on
"did it name the pathway" mostly measures whether the enrichment tool worked.

# 3. Mechanism recovery, hallucination and cost

```{r}
if (!is.null(bench)) {
  agg <- aggregate(cbind(recovery_keyword, recovery_judge, hallucination_rate,
                         cost_usd, completion_tokens, n_hypotheses) ~ model,
                   bench, mean, na.rm = TRUE, na.action = na.pass)
  agg$n_runs <- as.vector(table(bench$model)[agg$model])
  agg <- agg[order(-agg$recovery_keyword), c("model", "n_runs", setdiff(names(agg), c("model", "n_runs")))]
  knitr::kable(agg, digits = 4,
    caption = "Mean performance per model over the completed runs. `n_runs` is given because a mean over one run is a single observation, not an estimate.")
}
```

```{r fig.height=3.4}
if (!is.null(bench) && nrow(bench) > 1) {
  ggplot(bench, aes(reorder(dataset, recovery_keyword), recovery_keyword,
                    fill = model)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.82), width = 0.75) +
    coord_flip() + ylim(0, 1) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "mechanism recovery rate", fill = "model",
         title = "Recovery of the pre-registered mechanism, by dataset")
}
```

```{r}
if (!is.null(bench)) {
  knitr::kable(
    bench[, c("dataset", "model", "recovery_keyword", "recovery_judge",
              "hallucination_rate", "n_hypotheses", "prompt_tokens",
              "completion_tokens", "cost_usd", "elapsed_sec")],
    digits = 4,
    caption = "Per-run detail. recovery_judge is NA unless RUN_JUDGE=1 (cross-model judge).")
  cat(sprintf(
    "\nTotal measured spend across all completed runs: **$%.4f**; median cost per dataset-model run **$%.4f**.\n",
    sum(bench$cost_usd, na.rm = TRUE), median(bench$cost_usd, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
```

## 3.1 Hallucination

```{r fig.height=2.9}
if (!is.null(bench)) {
  ggplot(bench, aes(model, hallucination_rate, fill = model)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.55) + facet_wrap(~ dataset) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "hallucination rate",
         title = "Cited pathways present in neither the input table nor the vocabulary") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), legend.position = "none")
}
```

Every completed run scores **0** — no pathway was invented that was absent
from both the input enrichment table and the controlled vocabulary. This is
by construction rather than luck: the schema constrains `supporting_pathways`
to the provided table, and `validate_terms()` re-checks each cited term after
generation and records the violation rate instead of trusting the model's
compliance. A zero here is evidence that the *audit* works, not that the model
is honest; the guard is what makes the number meaningful.

# 4. Ablation: what the user actually controls

Three knobs are exposed by `interpret_enrichment()`: whether a few-shot
exemplar is included, how many pathways are shown (`top_n`), and whether
tissue context is supplied. `benchmark/03_run_ablation.R` runs the full
3-dataset × 2 × 4 × 2 = 48-cell grid.

```{r fig.height=3.4}
if (!is.null(abl)) {
  a <- aggregate(recovery_keyword ~ top_n + few_shot + tissue, abl, mean)
  ggplot(a, aes(factor(top_n), recovery_keyword, colour = factor(few_shot),
                group = few_shot)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1.6) + facet_wrap(~ tissue) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = "pathways shown to the model (top_n)", y = "mean recovery rate",
         colour = "few-shot", title = "Ablation grid, 3 datasets pooled")
}
```

```{r}
if (!is.null(abl)) {
  marg <- rbind(
    data.frame(factor = "few-shot exemplar", level = c("off", "on"),
               recovery = tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$few_shot, mean)[c("FALSE","TRUE")],
               hallucination = tapply(abl$hallucination_rate, abl$few_shot, mean)[c("FALSE","TRUE")],
               prompt_tokens = tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, abl$few_shot, mean)[c("FALSE","TRUE")]),
    data.frame(factor = "pathways shown",
               level = as.character(sort(unique(abl$top_n))),
               recovery = tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, factor(abl$top_n, levels = sort(unique(abl$top_n))), mean),
               hallucination = tapply(abl$hallucination_rate, factor(abl$top_n, levels = sort(unique(abl$top_n))), mean),
               prompt_tokens = tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, factor(abl$top_n, levels = sort(unique(abl$top_n))), mean)),
    data.frame(factor = "tissue context", level = c("absent", "present"),
               recovery = tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$tissue, mean)[c("FALSE","TRUE")],
               hallucination = tapply(abl$hallucination_rate, abl$tissue, mean)[c("FALSE","TRUE")],
               prompt_tokens = tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, abl$tissue, mean)[c("FALSE","TRUE")]))
  rownames(marg) <- NULL
  knitr::kable(marg, digits = 3,
    caption = "Marginal means for each prompt-design factor (48 configurations).")
}
```

Three findings, in decreasing order of how much they surprised us:

1. **Few-shot exemplars hurt.** Mean recovery drops from
   `r sprintf("%.2f", tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$few_shot, mean)[1])`
   to `r sprintf("%.2f", tapply(abl$recovery_keyword, abl$few_shot, mean)[2])`
   while prompt tokens rise `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, abl$few_shot, mean)[2] / tapply(abl$prompt_tokens, abl$few_shot, mean)[1] - 1))`.
   The exemplar anchors the model on the example's biology: it copies the
   *shape* of the demonstration instead of the dataset's own evidence. Few-shot
   prompting is the default advice for structured output, and here it is a net
   loss on both axes.
2. **More pathways is better.** Recovery rises monotonically from `top_n = 10`
   to `top_n = 30`. Truncating the enrichment table to the "top 5 significant
   hits" — the usual display convention — removes exactly the context the model
   needs to judge which pathway is causal.
3. **Tissue context is close to neutral**, which is a mild argument for keeping
   it: it costs few tokens and adds a prior that occasionally prevents an
   organ-specific misreading.

# 5. Worked example

```{r}
if (!is.null(bench)) {
  ex <- bench[which.max(bench$recovery_keyword), ]
  r <- readRDS(file.path("results", paste0(
    ex$dataset, "__", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]", "-", as.character(ex$model)), ".rds")))
  cat(sprintf("**%s on `%s`** (%s DEGs, %.0f%% recovery)\n\n",
              as.character(ex$model), ex$dataset, r$deg_mode,
              100 * ex$recovery_keyword))
  for (h in r$interpretation$hypotheses) {
    cat("- **", h$name, "** (", h$evidence_grade, ") — ", h$mechanism, "\n", sep = "")
    cat("  - supported by: ", paste(unlist(h$supporting_pathways), collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "")
    cat("  - driver genes: ", paste(unlist(h$driver_genes)[1:6], collapse = ", "), "\n", sep = "")
    cat("  - proposed test: ", h$follow_up_experiment, "\n", sep = "")
  }
  cat("\nGround truth for this dataset: ",
      gsub("\\|", "; ", gt$gt_components[gt$dataset_id == ex$dataset]), "\n", sep = "")
}
```

# 6. Failure modes observed

Where the pipeline is wrong, it is wrong in ways a reader can see:

- **Direction inversion.** With a weak contrast (rapamycin NK, `top-150`
  fallback) the recovered pathway is right but the inferred direction of
  regulation is not. The score is unaffected — component matching is
  direction-agnostic — which is a known limitation of the current metric, not
  of the model.
- **Passenger pathway promotion.** In the imatinib K562 run, cell-cycle terms
  are ranked above the BCR-ABL/JAK-STAT axis because proliferation shutdown
  dominates the DE list. ORA cannot distinguish the drug's target from its
  consequence; the model frequently can, and when it cannot, the ranking is
  where it shows.
- **Schema compliance is not free.** DeepSeek's JSON mode requires the literal
  string "json" in the prompt and rejects a schema-less request. `call_llm()`
  therefore requests JSON only when a schema is supplied; without that rule the
  call fails with a 400 rather than degrading.

# 7. What this benchmark does not establish

- **No generalisation claim across model families.** Only DeepSeek endpoints
  are covered by the runs completed so far; `models.csv` is provider-agnostic,
  but a same-vendor comparison cannot speak to whether the findings hold for
  other vendors.
- **Ground truth is coarse.** Three components per dataset is enough to catch
  gross failure, not enough to distinguish a good interpretation from a very
  good one. The judge score helps but is itself model-dependent.
- **Single annotator projection.** The `expected_gmt` mapping is one expert's
  projection of the mechanism onto 49 terms. It is applied identically to both
  arms, which protects the comparison but not the absolute recovery number.
- **No wet-lab validation.** Every "follow-up experiment" in the output is a
  proposal, and none was performed.

# 8. Reproducibility

- **Caching.** Every LLM call is hashed on prompt + model + temperature and
  stored on disk (`R/llm-backend.R`), so this document can be regenerated
  without re-spending budget, and a re-run with the same inputs is
  byte-identical.
- **Pinned inputs.** `benchmark/00_fetch_geo.sh` records the archive sizes it
  expects and fails loudly on a truncated download; `ground_truth.csv` is
  version-controlled and its history shows the mechanism text was frozen
  before the first model call.
- **Adaptive DE rule is logged, not silent.** `deg_mode` and `n_degs` are
  written into every result file, so a reader can always see whether a run used
  strict thresholds or the top-150 fallback.
- **Scoring is two-track.** A deterministic synonym-aware matcher (free,
  reproducible) and a cross-model judge (paid, bias-reduced). Disagreement
  between the two tracks is reported rather than averaged away.
